# Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
*Homo erectus* was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, *Homo*, took over the world.
## A handful of teeth with a lot to say
Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there.
The hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.
## Tracing how Homo erectus populations moved around
While the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly *Homo erectus*, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian *Homo erectus* fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced.

There, they discovered more than 10,000 fossil teeth from animals such as orangutans (*Pongo* spp.), monkeys and wild boar (*Sus* spp.), as well as 9 from hominins. The researchers estimate that the hominins lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago, according to dating of both fossils and the surrounding sediments using various methods.

Lofty mountaintops. Arid deserts. Frozen tundras.

Modern humans call nearly environment on Earth home. Turns out our distant ancestors may have, too.

A recent analysis of very old teeth found in southern China suggests that Homo erectus survived in the dense tropical rainforests of the region, adapting to conditions previously thought inhospitable for these hominins.

This very rigidity is what some scientists considered the downfall of Homo erectus. Those assumptions, though, now aren’t so clear.

seltz.title: Homo erectus Lived in China's Rainforests 184,000 Years Ago
seltz.snippet:
Nine ancient teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that *Homo erectus*, one of humanity's longest-lived relatives, held on in the region far longer than scientists believed and did so in dense rainforest. Two companion studies published in *Nature* on 18 November 2026 date the teeth to between about 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

The fossils come from the Baxian and Naxian caves near Chongzuo in Guangxi, close to China's border with Vietnam. According to Macquarie University's summary of the research, written by geochronologist Kira Westaway and co-authors, that is 100,000 to 200,000 years later than the species was thought to have survived in China.

The findings matter for two reasons. They give the youngest securely dated evidence of *H. erectus* in mainland China, and they offer the first direct evidence that the species lived in rainforest, a habitat long thought to be beyond it. The evidence still rests on a small number of teeth, and one tooth does not fit any known human species, which leaves an open question about who else lived in these forests.

### What the teeth revealed

*Homo erectus* first appeared about two million years ago and was the first member of the human genus known to spread from Africa into Asia. For decades, its Chinese record appeared to end several hundred thousand years ago. A 2026 review of the species' Chinese record put the known range at roughly 2.1 to 1.6 million years ago at the start and 400,000 to 300,000 years ago at the end. On the Indonesian island of Java, the species may have lasted until about 100,000 years ago.

The new teeth push the Chinese timeline much later. The research team identified eight of the nine teeth as *H. erectus*from their shape.
